claim: At vertebrate neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), the synaptic basal lamina contains different extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins and synaptogenic factors that induce and maintain synaptic specializations.
source: At vertebrate neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), the synaptic basal lamina contains different extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins and synaptogenic factors that induce and maintain synaptic specializations.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about NMJ structure and function, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Podosome-like structures (PLSs) induced by ubiquitous ECM proteins regulate the formation and remodeling of acetylcholine receptor (AChR) clusters via focal ECM degradation.
source: Here, we report that podosome-like structures (PLSs) induced by ubiquitous ECM proteins regulate the formation and remodeling of acetylcholine receptor (AChR) clusters via focal ECM degradation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing PLS localization at AChR clusters and ECM degradation patterns.

claim: ECM degradation is mediated by PLS-directed trafficking and surface insertion of membrane-type 1 matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP) to AChR clusters through microtubule-capturing mechanisms.
source: Mechanistically, ECM degradation is mediated by PLS-directed trafficking and surface insertion of membrane-type 1 matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP) to AChR clusters through microtubule-capturing mechanisms.
evidence: This mechanistic claim is supported by experimental data showing MT1-MMP trafficking, EB1/CLASP involvement, and surface insertion at AChR clusters.

claim: Upon synaptic induction, MT1-MMP plays a crucial role in the recruitment of aneural AChR clusters for the assembly of postsynaptic specializations.
source: Upon synaptic induction, MT1-MMP plays a crucial role in the recruitment of aneural AChR clusters for the assembly of postsynaptic specializations.
evidence: This is supported by photobleaching experiments showing differential recruitment of AChRs from aneural clusters versus diffuse pools, and MT1-MMP knockdown effects.

claim: The structural defects of NMJs in embryonic MT1-MMP-/- mice demonstrate the physiological role of MT1-MMP in normal NMJ development.
source: Lastly, the structural defects of NMJs in embryonic MT1-MMP-/- mice further demonstrate the physiological role of MT1-MMP in normal NMJ development.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data from MT1-MMP knockout mice showing altered aneural and synaptic AChR cluster densities.

claim: Postsynaptic MT1-MMP serves as a molecular switch to synaptogenesis by modulating local ECM environment for the deposition of synaptogenic signals that regulate postsynaptic differentiation at developing NMJs.
source: Collectively, this study suggests that postsynaptic MT1-MMP serves as a molecular switch to synaptogenesis by modulating local ECM environment for the deposition of synaptogenic signals that regulate postsynaptic differentiation at developing NMJs.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the collective experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: AChR molecules are clustered at a nearly crystalline density of ~10,000 receptors/μm2 at the postsynaptic apparatus of NMJs.
source: At the postsynaptic apparatus of NMJs, acetylcholine receptor (AChR) molecules are clustered at a nearly crystalline density of ~10,000 receptors/μm2 (Fertuck and Salpeter, 1976)
evidence: This is a cited fact from previous literature (Fertuck and Salpeter, 1976).

claim: AChR density drops drastically to <10 receptors/μm2 at the extra-synaptic regions.
source: in contrast, its density drops drastically to <10 receptors/μm2 at the extra-synaptic regions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AChR distribution at NMJs.

claim: Even in the absence of motor neurons, AChR clusters can still be found in muscle fibers in vivo.
source: Previous knockout studies showed that even in the absence of motor neurons, AChR clusters can still be found in muscle fibers in vivo (Lin et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous knockout studies (Lin et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001).

claim: AChR pre-patterns are spontaneously formed via muscle-intrinsic mechanisms.
source: suggesting that such AChR pre-patterns are spontaneously formed via muscle-intrinsic mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited knockout studies showing AChR clusters form without motor neurons.

claim: A similar structure of aneural AChR clusters can be induced in Xenopus primary muscles or immortalized C2C12 myotubes by culturing them on substratum coated with laminin.
source: Interestingly, a similar structure of aneural AChR clusters can be induced in Xenopus primary muscles or immortalized C2C12 myotubes by culturing them on substratum coated with laminin, a major structural glycoprotein in the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Kummer et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Kummer et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2009).

claim: Aneural AChR clusters located at the bottom surface of cultured muscles in direct contact with ECM proteins may undergo topological transformation, which is mirrored by the progressive structural changes in synaptic AChR clusters during NMJ maturation in vivo.
source: These aneural AChR clusters, located at the bottom surface of cultured muscles in direct contact with ECM proteins, may undergo topological transformation, which is mirrored by the progressive structural changes in synaptic AChR clusters during NMJ maturation in vivo (Kummer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kummer et al., 2004.

claim: Actin-rich structures are highly concentrated at the perforated regions of aneural AChR clusters.
source: Our previous work showed that actin-rich structures are highly concentrated at the perforated regions of aneural AChR clusters (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Lee et al., 2009).

claim: These structures share the typical characteristics of podosome-like structures (PLSs).
source: These structures were later shown to share the typical characteristics of podosome-like structures (PLSs) (Proszynski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Proszynski et al., 2009.

claim: PLSs have been linked to pathophysiological processes such as cancer cell invasion and metastasis via local proteolysis of ECM proteins.
source: PLSs, initially identified as dynamic foot-like structures in motile or invasive cells, have been linked to pathophysiological processes such as cancer cell invasion and metastasis via local proteolysis of ECM proteins (Linder, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Linder, 2007.

claim: A small proportion of aneural AChR clusters can be identified at the top surface of cultured muscles.
source: It is worth to note that a small proportion of aneural AChR clusters can also be identified at the top surface of cultured muscles
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Spontaneously formed clusters at the top surface are likely mediated through ECM- and PLS-independent mechanisms.
source: and these spontaneously formed clusters are likely mediated through ECM- and PLS-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that top clusters form without ECM contact.

claim: The assembly of PLSs can be induced by different ECM proteins.
source: In this study, we show that the assembly of PLSs, which can be induced by different ECM proteins, focally regulates matrix degradation for AChR clustering and topological remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PLS markers at AChR clusters on different ECM substrates.

claim: Intracellular trafficking and surface insertion of MT1-MMP are mediated via microtubule-capturing mechanisms at PLSs.
source: Next, we further demonstrate that intracellular trafficking and surface insertion of membrane-type 1 (MT1-) matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) are mediated via microtubule-capturing mechanisms at PLSs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing EB1/CLASP-dependent MT1-MMP trafficking and surface insertion.

claim: MT1-MMP spatiotemporally regulates the topological remodeling of aneural AChR clusters and their dispersal upon synaptic induction.
source: which in turn spatiotemporally regulate the topological remodeling of aneural AChR clusters and their dispersal upon synaptic induction.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing effects of MMP inhibitors and MT1-MMP knockdown on AChR cluster dynamics.

claim: Inhibition of MMP activity greatly suppresses nerve-induced AChR cluster formation.
source: Inhibition of MMP activity or reduced expression of muscle MT1-MMP greatly suppresses nerve-induced AChR cluster formation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from nerve-muscle co-cultures treated with MMP inhibitors.

claim: Inhibition of MMP activity stabilizes aneural AChR clusters against dispersal.
source: and stabilizes aneural AChR clusters against dispersal.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing reduced dispersal of aneural clusters with MMP inhibitor treatment.

claim: MT1-MMP is required for the recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural to synaptic AChR clusters at developing NMJs in vitro and in vivo.
source: Lastly, we show that MT1-MMP is required for the recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural to synaptic AChR clusters at developing NMJs in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by photobleaching experiments in vitro and analysis of MT1-MMP knockout mice in vivo.

claim: Topologically complex aneural AChR clusters were observed mostly on the bottom surface of muscle cells in contact with ECL-coated substratum.
source: When dissociated myotomal tissues from early Xenopus embryos were cultured on glass coverslips coated with a mixture of ECM proteins, containing entactin/nidogen, collagen and laminin (ECL), topologically complex aneural AChR clusters were observed mostly on the bottom surface of muscle cells in contact with ECL-coated substratum (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experiments and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Some aneural AChR clusters could be found within the top surface of muscle cells but exhibited a sparsely scattered morphology.
source: Some aneural AChR clusters could also be found within the top surface of muscle cells but exhibited a sparsely scattered morphology.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The formation of bottom AChR clusters could be effectively induced by laminin, collagen, and gelatin.
source: We found that the formation of bottom AChR clusters could be effectively induced by all ECM proteins tested, in contrast to the negative control using poly-D-lysine (PDL), a polypeptide commonly used to promote cell attachment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Poly-D-lysine (PDL) does not effectively induce bottom AChR clusters.
source: in contrast to the negative control using poly-D-lysine (PDL), a polypeptide commonly used to promote cell attachment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Aneural AChR clusters in C2C12 myotubes can undergo a topological transformation from a plaque to a perforated pretzel-shaped, and eventually to C-shaped arrays.
source: In immortalized C2C12 myotubes, aneural AChR clusters can undergo a topological transformation from a plaque to a perforated pretzel-shaped, and eventually to C-shaped arrays (Kummer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kummer et al., 2004.

claim: A majority of ECM-induced aneural AChR clusters exhibited perforated structures.
source: A majority of ECM-induced aneural AChR clusters exhibited perforated structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the classification of AChR cluster morphologies in the study.

claim: The percentage of muscle cells with AChR clusters was largely reduced on PDL-coated substrate.
source: While the percentage of muscle cells with AChR clusters was largely reduced on PDL-coated substrate, the largest share of AChR clusters exhibited scattered structures (9.59% out of 13.33% total) (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Most AChR clusters were gradually dispersed over 6 days in cultured Xenopus muscle cells.
source: As opposed to a previous study showing the topological transformation of AChR clusters in C2C12 myotubes (Kummer et al., 2004), most AChR clusters, regardless of their topological features, were gradually dispersed over 6 days in cultured Xenopus muscle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ADF/cofilin regulates the formation and maintenance of AChR clusters via vesicular trafficking.
source: Our previous study indicated that actin depolymerizing factor (ADF)/cofilin, one of the molecular components in PLSs, regulates the formation and maintenance of AChR clusters via vesicular trafficking (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Lee et al., 2009).

claim: All typical core and cortex markers of PLSs were found to be enriched in the perforations of AChR clusters in Xenopus muscle cultures.
source: Here, we further performed immunostaining of several typical core markers (composed of F-actin and actin-associated proteins, such as ADF/cofilin, Arp2/3 complex, and cortactin) and cortex markers (composed of adhesion molecules, such as vinculin, talin, and paxillin) of PLSs. All these markers were found to be enriched in the perforations (arrows) of AChR clusters in Xenopus muscle cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cortactin is highly enriched and involved in both early and late stages of PLS formation.
source: As cortactin is highly enriched and involved in both early and late stages of PLS formation (Webb et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Webb et al., 2006.

claim: PLSs were spatially concentrated in a majority of perforated AChR clusters induced by different ECM proteins.
source: PLSs were spatially concentrated in a majority of perforated AChR clusters induced by different ECM proteins (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 1D and E.

claim: PLSs were not localized in AChR clusters on PDL substrates.
source: In contrast, PLSs were not localized in AChR clusters, even in a small fraction of AChR clusters (2.16% out of 13.33% total) exhibiting perforated structures, on PDL substrates.
evidence: This is an observation from the quantitative analysis of cortactin localization.

claim: Different ECM proteins can induce the assembly of PLSs, which may in turn promote the formation of topologically complex structures of AChR clusters.
source: These data suggest that different ECM proteins can induce the assembly of PLSs, which may in turn promote the formation of topologically complex structures of AChR clusters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations showing PLS localization at perforated AChR clusters induced by various ECM proteins.

claim: Perforated AChR clusters can be effectively induced by gelatin.
source: The data above showed that perforated AChR clusters can be effectively induced by gelatin (Figure 1B and C)
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Gelatin was previously shown to induce simple AChR plaques only.
source: an ECM protein that was previously shown to induce simple AChR plaques only (Kummer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kummer et al., 2004.

claim: FITC-gelatin was extensively degraded in close association with the perforated regions of aneural AChR clusters.
source: We observed FITC-gelatin that was extensively degraded in close association with the perforated regions of aneural AChR clusters (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal microscopy images presented in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a linear relationship between the extent of gelatin degradation and the perforation area of aneural AChR clusters.
source: Next, we quantitatively measured the fluorescence intensity of FITC-gelatin in different AChR clusters and identified a linear relationship between the extent of gelatin degradation and the perforation area of aneural AChR clusters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: A similar spatially restricted gelatin degradation pattern was observed in cultured C2C12 myotubes.
source: A similar spatially restricted gelatin degradation pattern was observed in cultured C2C12 myotubes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the images presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Immunostaining experiments showed the spatial degradation of laminin at the perforated regions of AChR clusters in Xenopus primary muscle cells.
source: Besides gelatin, immunostaining experiments also showed the spatial degradation of laminin at the perforated regions of AChR clusters in Xenopus primary muscle cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: BB-94 and BB-2516 are highly potent against MMP-1, -2, -3, -7, -9 and MT1-MMP.
source: To examine if the focal degradation pattern of ECM proteins is mediated by MMP activity, we first used two broad-spectrum MMP inhibitors, BB-94 and Marimastat (BB-2516), which are known to be highly potent against MMP-1, -2, -3, -7, -9 and MT1-MMP (Cathcart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cathcart et al., 2015.

claim: The degradation of fluorescent gelatin associated with perforated AChR clusters was completely abolished by BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment.
source: Although perforated AChR clusters could be identified in muscle cells treated with 5 µM BB-94 or 10 µM BB-2516, the degradation of fluorescent gelatin associated with these perforated AChR clusters was completely abolished (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The initial formation of aneural AChR clusters in muscle cells was largely unaffected in the presence of MMP inhibitors.
source: Quantification further demonstrated that the initial formation of aneural AChR clusters in muscle cells was largely unaffected in the presence of MMP inhibitors (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 2G.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of aneural AChR clusters in control muscle cells over 2 days.
source: We observed a significant reduction in the number of aneural AChR clusters in control muscle cells, in contrast to BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment that caused a slight increase in the number of aneural AChR clusters (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 2H.

claim: BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment caused a slight increase in the number of aneural AChR clusters.
source: in contrast to BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment that caused a slight increase in the number of aneural AChR clusters (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 2H.

claim: In control untreated cells, there was a gradual dispersal of aneural AChR clusters over the 96 hr imaging period.
source: In control untreated cells, we observed a gradual dispersal of aneural AChR clusters over the 96 hr imaging period; however, such spontaneous dispersal and topological remodeling of AChR clusters were largely inhibited by BB-94 treatment within the same imaging period (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse imaging data presented in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Spontaneous dispersal and topological remodeling of AChR clusters were largely inhibited by BB-94 treatment.
source: however, such spontaneous dispersal and topological remodeling of AChR clusters were largely inhibited by BB-94 treatment within the same imaging period (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse imaging data presented in Figure 2I and J.

claim: MMP activity is involved in the topological remodeling and dispersal of aneural AChR clusters.
source: These data demonstrated that MMP activity is involved in the topological remodeling and dispersal of aneural AChR clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing effects of MMP inhibitors on AChR cluster dynamics.

claim: Endogenous MT1-MMP was enriched in the perforations of aneural AChR clusters.
source: To test this, we first performed immunostaining of Xenopus muscle cells and detected endogenous MT1-MMP that was enriched in the perforations of aneural AChR clusters (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: In MT1-MMP-mCherry-overexpressing muscle cells, there was extensive degradation of fluorescent gelatin in the entire cell area.
source: In MT1-MMP-mCherry-overexpressing muscle cells, we observed extensive degradation of fluorescent gelatin in the entire cell area (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: MT1-MMP-mCherry overexpressing cells showed a lower percentage of ECM-induced bottom AChR clusters, but a higher percentage of top AChR clusters, in comparison to the wild-type control cells.
source: In addition, MT1-MMP-mCherry overexpressing cells showed a lower percentage of ECM-induced bottom AChR clusters, but a higher percentage of top AChR clusters, in comparison to the wild-type control cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The intensity of aneural AChR clusters was significantly reduced in MT1-MMP-mCherry-overexpressing cells, which was accompanied by the extensive gelatin degradation.
source: Quantitative analyses on those bottom AChR clusters in MT1-MMP-mCherry-overexpressing cells showed that the intensity of aneural AChR clusters was significantly reduced, which was accompanied by the extensive gelatin degradation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment was able to partially revert the distribution of aneural AChR clusters from the top surface back to the bottom surface of MT1-MMP-mCherry-overexpressing muscle cells.
source: Interestingly, BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment was able to partially revert the distribution of aneural AChR clusters from the top surface back to the bottom surface of MT1-MMP-mCherry-overexpressing muscle cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The extensive degradation of fluorescent gelatin and the reduction of AChR intensity caused by MT1-MMP-mCherry overexpression were largely rescued by either BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment.
source: Consistent with that, the extensive degradation of fluorescent gelatin and the reduction of AChR intensity caused by MT1-MMP-mCherry overexpression were largely rescued by either BB-94 or BB-2516 treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The precise control of focal ECM degradation by MT1-MMP at the perforated sites plays an essential role in the formation of bottom aneural AChR clusters.
source: Our results indicated that the precise control of focal ECM degradation by MT1-MMP at the perforated sites plays an essential role in the formation of bottom aneural AChR clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing effects of MT1-MMP overexpression and MMP inhibitors.

claim: EB1-GFP comets were highly enriched at the perforated aneural AChR clusters.
source: Interestingly, we observed EB1-GFP comets to be highly enriched at the perforated aneural AChR clusters (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the TIRF microscopy data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: A similar localization pattern of endogenous EB1 signals was detected in fixed Xenopus muscle cells.
source: This pattern of EB1-GFP comets was not an artifact of overexpression, as a similar localization pattern of endogenous EB1 signals was also detected in fixed Xenopus muscle cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EB1-GFP comets were densely localized, but they showed lower mobility, at sites of aneural AChR clusters than other regions of the cell.
source: By analyzing the density and trajectory of EB1-GFP comets in time-lapse images, we found that EB1-GFP comets were densely localized, but they showed lower mobility, at sites of aneural AChR clusters than other regions of the cell (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative analysis presented in Figure 4B and C.

claim: AChR clusters are the focal point of directed microtubule-based intracellular transport.
source: These data suggested that AChR clusters are the focal point of directed microtubule-based intracellular transport.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of enriched and less mobile EB1 comets at AChR clusters.

claim: CLASP and LL5β interact with microtubules to direct the vesicular trafficking of different proteins to the NMJ.
source: Previous studies showed that cytoplasmic linker-associated protein (CLASP) and LL5β, a PLS cortex protein involved in NMJ development (Kishi et al., 2005), interact with microtubules to direct the vesicular trafficking of different proteins to the NMJ (Basu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kishi et al., 2005 and Basu et al., 2015.

claim: Endogenous CLASP protein level was largely reduced in Xenopus embryos microinjected with CLASP-MO.
source: As validated by western blot analysis, endogenous CLASP protein level was largely reduced in Xenopus embryos microinjected with CLASP-MO (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the western blot data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In CLASP-MO muscle cells, the perimembrane signals of EB1-GFP were primarily found at the center of perforations within aneural AChR clusters.
source: In CLASP-MO muscle cells, TIRF microscopy showed the perimembrane signals of EB1-GFP that were primarily found at the center of perforations within aneural AChR clusters (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the TIRF microscopy data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The density of EB1-GFP comets was only slightly reduced at AChR cluster region in CLASP-MO muscle cells.
source: Although the density of EB1-GFP comets was only slightly reduced at AChR cluster region (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The average speed of EB1-GFP comets in the region of AChR clusters was significantly increased by 26.7% to 0.12 ± 0.004 μm/s in CLASP-MO muscle cells.
source: the average speed of EB1-GFP comets in the region of AChR clusters was significantly increased by 26.7% to 0.12 ± 0.004 μm/s in CLASP-MO muscle cells (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: CLASP is involved in microtubule capturing at aneural AChR clusters.
source: indicating that CLASP is involved in microtubule capturing at aneural AChR clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of increased EB1 comet speed in CLASP knockdown cells.

claim: Before photobleaching, EB1-GFP signals were primarily enriched at the edge of perforations of aneural AChR clusters in control cells but at the center of perforations in CLASP-MO muscle cells.
source: Before photobleaching, EB1-GFP signals were primarily enriched at the edge of perforations of aneural AChR clusters in control cells but at the center of perforations in CLASP-MO muscle cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in the TIRF microscopy data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: In the control cell, the peaks of EB1-GFP intensity showed a slight lateral shift towards the center of a perforated region.
source: In the control cell, the peaks of EB1-GFP intensity showed a slight lateral shift towards the center of a perforated region (Top chart, Figure 4E)
evidence: This is shown in the line profile analysis presented in Figure 4E.

claim: CLASP knockdown caused the peak of EB1-GFP intensity to cover a larger area of a perforated region.
source: In contrast, CLASP knockdown caused the peak of EB1-GFP intensity to cover a larger area of a perforated region, indicating that EB1-GFP is enriched relatively closer to the center of perforations (Bottom chart, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in the line profile analysis presented in Figure 4E.

claim: The recovery of EB1-GFP signals was detected near the edge of perforations within AChR clusters in control cells.
source: Spatially, the recovery of EB1-GFP signals was detected near the edge of those perforations within AChR clusters in control cells (arrows in Figure 4F, Figure 4—video 1)
evidence: This is shown in the FRAP data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: The recovery of EB1-GFP signals was largely reduced in CLASP-MO muscle cells.
source: but it was largely reduced in CLASP-MO muscle cells (arrowheads in Figure 4F, Figure 4—video 2)
evidence: This is shown in the FRAP data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: CLASP knockdown led to a significant increase in the half-time of EB1-GFP signal recovery by 58% from 5.71 ± 0.83 s in control cells to 9.01 ± 0.71 s in CLASP-MO muscle cells.
source: leading to a significant increase in the half-time of EB1-GFP signal recovery by 58% from 5.71 ± 0.83 s in control cells to 9.01 ± 0.71 s in CLASP-MO muscle cells (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative FRAP analysis presented in Figure 4G and H.

claim: PLSs may direct the vesicular trafficking to AChR clusters through EB1-/CLASP-mediated microtubule-capturing mechanisms.
source: Collectively, our data suggested that PLSs may direct the vesicular trafficking to AChR clusters through EB1-/CLASP-mediated microtubule-capturing mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on EB1 localization and CLASP knockdown effects.

claim: Some MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles were found to be initially immobile until they were captured by a moving EB1-GFP comet.
source: In region 'i', some MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles (arrows) were found to be initially immobile at the beginning of this time-lapse series, until they were captured by a moving EB1-GFP comet (arrowhead), leading to a coordinated movement of both EB1-GFP and MT1-MMP-mCherry signals from 27 s to 29 s time-points in this imaging period (middle row, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse imaging data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles were able to move bidirectionally on microtubule structures.
source: Another example in region 'ii' indicated that MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles (arrows) were able to move bidirectionally on microtubule structures, as visualized by the fading tracks (arrowheads) generated by moving EB1-GFP comets (bottom row, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse imaging data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Most MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles were found to be relatively immobile in kymographs.
source: In these two kymographs, most MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles were found to be relatively immobile.
evidence: This is an observation from the kymograph analysis.

claim: Some displacement of MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles was observed immediately after EB1-GFP comets had come into contact with them.
source: Interestingly, we observed some displacement of MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles immediately after EB1-GFP comets had come into contact with them (arrows in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the kymograph analysis presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Endogenous MT1-MMP exhibited punctuated structures inside the muscle cells, and some of them were co-localized with vesicle-associated membrane protein 1 (VAMP1).
source: Consistent with the subcellular localization of MT1-MMP-mCherry, immunostaining data revealed that endogenous MT1-MMP exhibited punctuated structures inside the muscle cells, and some of them were co-localized with vesicle-associated membrane protein 1 (VAMP1) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: EB1 coordinates the vesicular trafficking of MT1-MMP in cultured muscle cells.
source: Taken together, these data illustrated that EB1 coordinates the vesicular trafficking of MT1-MMP in cultured muscle cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-lapse imaging and kymograph data showing coordinated movement of EB1 and MT1-MMP.

claim: Local capturing of MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles was detected at the edge of perforations within aneural AChR clusters.
source: After photobleaching, we detected local capturing of MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles at the edge of perforations within aneural AChR clusters (white arrows, region 'i' in Figure 5C)
evidence: This is shown in the TIRF-FRAP data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Local capturing of MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles was detected at the edge of AChR cluster periphery.
source: as well as at the edge of AChR cluster periphery (red and green arrows, region 'ii' in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in the TIRF-FRAP data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles were frequently captured at both perforations and periphery of AChR clusters over the 120 s imaging period after photobleaching.
source: In kymographs constructed along 'K3' and 'K4' lines, we observed MT1-MMP-mCherry vesicles that were frequently captured at both perforations (arrowheads) and periphery (arrows) of AChR clusters over the 120 s imaging period after photobleaching (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the kymograph analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: PLSs, through the cortex domains, can mediate site-directed capturing of MT1-MMP vesicles for their subsequent surface insertion.
source: As both sites are enriched with PLS cortex markers, vinculin and talin (arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we speculated that PLSs, through the cortex domains, can mediate site-directed capturing of MT1-MMP vesicles for their subsequent surface insertion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of MT1-MMP capture at sites enriched with PLS cortex markers.

claim: In cultured muscle with low MT1-MMP-pHluorin expression level, MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals were spatially enriched at the perforated regions of aneural AChR clusters.
source: In cultured muscle with low MT1-MMP-pHluorin expression level, MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals were spatially enriched at the perforated regions of aneural AChR clusters (arrow ) and caused only a slight inhibition on aneural AChR clustering (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the imaging data presented in Figure 6A and B.

claim: At high MT1-MMP-pHluorin expression, the formation of AChR bottom clusters was significantly inhibited.
source: At high MT1-MMP-pHluorin expression, the formation of AChR bottom clusters was significantly inhibited, leading to sparsely scattered appearance if observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with high MT1-MMP-pHluorin expression.

claim: MT1-MMP activity is crucial for the formation of topologically complex AChR clusters by precisely controlling focal ECM degradation at the perforated sites.
source: These data further confirmed that MT1-MMP activity is crucial for the formation of topologically complex AChR clusters by precisely controlling focal ECM degradation at the perforated sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MT1-MMP-pHluorin overexpression experiments.

claim: Treatment with a non-permeable buffer at pH 5.0 caused a large reduction in MT1-MMP-pHluorin fluorescence intensity.
source: To validate the surface localization of MT1-MMP in AChR clusters, we treated MT1-MMP-pHluorin-expressing muscle cells with a non-permeable buffer at pH 5.0 and observed a large reduction in MT1-MMP-pHluorin fluorescence intensity (arrows in Figure 6C)
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The signals were restored after changing the culture medium back to pH 7.8.
source: The signals were then restored after changing the culture medium back to pH 7.8, validating the effectiveness of this probe for visualizing surface localization of MT1-MMP, as it emits bright fluorescence upon surface insertion.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data validating the pH-sensitive probe.

claim: AChR cluster intensity was moderately reduced by 26% after 24 hr in the muscle cell with a very low expression level of MT1-MMP-pHluorin.
source: In this example, AChR cluster intensity was moderately reduced by 26% after 24 hr in the muscle cell with a very low expression level of MT1-MMP-pHluorin.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-lapse imaging experiment.

claim: AChR cluster intensity in a muscle cell with a relatively higher (low) MT1-MMP-pHluorin expression showed about 78% reduction during the same period.
source: In contrast, AChR cluster intensity in a muscle cell with a relatively higher (low) MT1-MMP-pHluorin expression showed about 78% reduction during the same period.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-lapse imaging experiment.

claim: MT1-MMP-pHluorin intensity in AChR cluster region was linearly correlated with the change in AChR cluster intensity over the next 24 hr.
source: Quantitative analyses on a pool data of 13 AChR clusters further indicated that MT1-MMP-pHluorin intensity in AChR cluster region was linearly correlated with the change in AChR cluster intensity over the next 24 hr (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot analysis presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Surface MT1-MMP has a functional role in promoting the topological remodeling of AChR clusters.
source: These data indicated the functional role of surface MT1-MMP in promoting the topological remodeling of AChR clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between MT1-MMP-pHluorin intensity and AChR cluster remodeling.

claim: Strong and discrete MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals re-appeared at the perforation and periphery of AChR clusters after photo-bleaching in control muscle cells.
source: In this example, strong and discrete MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals re-appeared at the perforation (arrows) and periphery (arrowheads) of AChR clusters at time-points of 118 s and 48 s, respectively, in control muscle cells after photo-bleaching (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in the TIRF-FRAP data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: Some newly inserted MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals were relatively stable.
source: Kymographs constructed along 'K1' and 'K2' lines indicated that some newly inserted MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals were relatively stable (arrows)
evidence: This is shown in the kymograph analysis presented in Figure 6G.

claim: Some newly inserted MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals were short-lived but with multiple events of MT1-MMP surface insertion at the same location in AChR clusters.
source: while some were short-lived but with multiple events of MT1-MMP surface insertion at the same location in AChR clusters (arrowheads) within a short imaging period (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in the kymograph analysis presented in Figure 6G.

claim: There was a significant reduction of MT1-MMP-pHluorin surface insertion at AChR clusters in CLASP-MO muscle cells when compared to that in control cells.
source: By quantifying the number of events of MT1-MMP surface insertion, we detected a significant reduction of MT1-MMP-pHluorin surface insertion at AChR clusters in CLASP-MO muscle cells when compared to that in control cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 6H.

claim: Vesicular trafficking and surface targeting of MT1-MMP are spatially regulated by PLS cortex proteins at the perforation and periphery of AChR clusters through EB1-/CLASP-mediated microtubule capturing mechanisms.
source: Together with the above data showing the local capture of EB1-GFP comets, this data further confirmed that vesicular trafficking and surface targeting of MT1-MMP are spatially regulated by PLS cortex proteins at the perforation and periphery of AChR clusters through EB1-/CLASP-mediated microtubule capturing mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on EB1 capture and MT1-MMP surface insertion.

claim: Spatial degradation of fluorescent gelatin-coated substratum and synaptic AChR clustering were observed at the nerve-muscle contacts.
source: Along the trail of neurites in contact with the basal membrane of muscle cells (arrows), we observed spatial degradation of fluorescent gelatin-coated substratum and synaptic AChR clustering at the nerve-muscle contacts (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in the imaging data from nerve-muscle co-cultures presented in Figure 7A.

claim: Synaptic AChR clusters at the nerve-muscle contacts were found to be closely associated to, but not perfectly co-localized with, the sites of gelatin degradation.
source: Like the focal gelatin degradation patterns observed in AChR-poor regions of aneural clusters (Figure 2A), synaptic AChR clusters at the nerve-muscle contacts were found to be closely associated to, but not perfectly co-localized with, the sites of gelatin degradation, with only 17.15 ± 15% of area in AChR clusters to be associated with gelatin degradation in control co-cultures (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative analysis presented in Figure 7C.

claim: Both gelatin degradation and nerve-induced AChR clustering were effectively inhibited by BB-94 or BB-2516.
source: However, both gelatin degradation and nerve-induced AChR clustering were effectively inhibited by BB-94 or BB-2516 (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Nerve innervation of skeletal muscles involves local signals to initiate the formation of synaptic AChR clusters and global signals to induce the dispersal of aneural AChR clusters.
source: Nerve innervation of skeletal muscles involves local signals to initiate the formation of synaptic AChR clusters and global signals to induce the dispersal of aneural AChR clusters (Dai and Peng, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dai and Peng, 1998.

claim: In control cells, there was a gradual dispersal of aneural AChR clusters upon agrin-bead stimulation for 24 hr.
source: In control cells, we detected a gradual dispersal of aneural AChR clusters upon agrin-bead stimulation for 24 hr
evidence: This is an observation from the agrin bead stimulation experiments.

claim: Aneural AChR clusters in agrin bead-contacted muscle cells were greatly stabilized by BB-94 or BB-2516.
source: however, those clusters in agrin bead-contacted muscle cells were greatly stabilized by BB-94 or BB-2516 (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Agrin stimulation enhances the localization of endogenous MT1-MMP in aneural AChR clusters prior to their dispersal.
source: To determine if agrin stimulation enhances the localization of MT1-MMP in aneural AChR clusters prior to their dispersal, we performed immunostaining experiments, in which we demonstrated an increase of endogenous MT1-MMP signals at aneural AChR clusters upon agrin stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: MT1-MMP activity plays an important role in regulating the assembly of synaptic AChR clusters at nerve-muscle contacts and the disassembly of aneural AChR clusters at developing NMJs.
source: These data implicated the important role of MT1-MMP activity in regulating not only the assembly of synaptic AChR clusters at nerve-muscle contacts, but also the disassembly of aneural AChR clusters, at developing NMJs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on MMP inhibitor effects in nerve-muscle co-cultures and agrin stimulation.

claim: MMP inhibitors did not significantly affect the formation of AChR clusters induced by agrin beads.
source: In contrast to nerve-induced AChR clustering, we noted that MMP inhibitors did not significantly affect the formation of AChR clusters induced by agrin beads (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Both BB-94 and BB-2516 significantly inhibited the formation of synaptic AChR clusters induced by the endogenous agrin tracks.
source: Using this assay, both BB-94 and BB-2516 were found to significantly inhibit the formation of synaptic AChR clusters induced by the endogenous agrin tracks (Figure 7F and G)
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data from the endogenous agrin track assay presented in Figure 7F and G.

claim: MT1-MMP knockdown caused a significant reduction, but not a complete inhibition, of nerve-induced AChR clustering in the chimeric co-cultures of MT1-MMP MO muscles with WT neurons.
source: Importantly, MT1-MMP knockdown caused a significant reduction, but not a complete inhibition, of nerve-induced AChR clustering in the chimeric co-cultures of MT1-MMP MO muscles with WT neurons (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data from chimeric co-cultures presented in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Both pre-existing and newly inserted AChRs at the nerve-muscle contacts were equally affected in the chimeric co-cultures of MT1-MMP MO muscles with WT neurons.
source: Intriguingly, both pre-existing and newly inserted AChRs at the nerve-muscle contacts were equally affected in the chimeric co-cultures of MT1-MMP MO muscles with WT neurons (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data presented in Figure 8C and D.

claim: In the chimeric co-cultures of MT1-MO + MT1-mCherry muscles with WT neurons, the percentage of nerve-muscle contacts with AChR clusters was largely returned to the level comparable with the control groups.
source: In the chimeric co-cultures of MT1-MO + MT1-mCherry muscles with WT neurons, we found that the percentage of nerve-muscle contacts with AChR clusters was largely returned to the level comparable with the control groups, and both pre-existing and newly inserted AChRs were detected at the nerve-muscle contacts (Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiment data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Postsynaptic MT1-MMP regulates both the surface delivery of newly synthesized AChR molecules and the redistribution/recruitment of pre-existing AChR molecules during the assembly of nerve-induced postsynaptic specializations at developing NMJs.
source: These data suggested that postsynaptic MT1-MMP regulates both the surface delivery of newly synthesized AChR molecules and the redistribution/recruitment of pre-existing AChR molecules (from either aneural AChR clusters or diffuse AChRs on muscle surface) during the assembly of nerve-induced postsynaptic specializations at developing NMJs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimeric co-culture experiments showing effects on both pre-existing and newly inserted AChRs.

claim: Without photobleaching, AChR signals were prominently detected at the nerve-muscle contact sites.
source: Without photobleaching, AChR signals were prominently detected at the nerve-muscle contact sites.
evidence: This is an observation from the photobleaching experiments.

claim: The formation of nerve-induced synaptic AChR clusters was accompanied by the dispersal of aneural AChR clusters after 1 day in co-culture.
source: The formation of nerve-induced synaptic AChR clusters was accompanied by the dispersal of aneural AChR clusters after 1 day in co-culture.
evidence: This is an observation from the nerve-muscle co-culture experiments.

claim: In the experimental groups with photobleaching of aneural AChR clusters before co-culturing with the spinal neurons, there was a significant reduction in AChR signals at the nerve-muscle contacts in comparison to the control groups without photobleaching.
source: In the experimental groups with photobleaching of aneural AChR clusters before co-culturing with the spinal neurons, we detected a significant reduction in AChR signals, which were contributed from diffuse AChRs only, at the nerve-muscle contacts in comparison to the control groups without photobleaching (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the photobleaching experiment data presented in Figure 9B and C.

claim: AChR molecules from aneural clusters serve as a major source for the assembly of synaptic AChR clusters.
source: These results provided compelling evidence to support the hypothesis that AChR molecules from aneural clusters serve as a major source for the assembly of synaptic AChR clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the photobleaching experiments showing reduced synaptic AChR signals when aneural clusters are photobleached.

claim: In the chimeric co-cultures with control MO muscle cells, both aneural clustered and diffuse AChRs were recruited to the nerve-muscle contacts at a level comparable to the wild-type co-cultures.
source: In the chimeric co-cultures with control MO muscle cells, both aneural clustered and diffuse AChRs were recruited to the nerve-muscle contacts at a level comparable to the wild-type co-cultures.
evidence: This is an observation from the chimeric co-culture experiments with control MO.

claim: Knockdown of MT1-MMP in muscles significantly suppressed the recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural to synaptic clusters, while the recruitment from diffuse AChRs was unaffected.
source: However, knockdown of MT1-MMP in muscles significantly suppressed the recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural to synaptic clusters, while the recruitment from diffuse AChRs was unaffected (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data from photobleaching experiments in MT1-MMP knockdown co-cultures presented in Figure 9C.

claim: Knockdown of muscle MT1-MMP caused a higher stability of aneural AChR clusters against nerve-induced dispersal.
source: Consistent with the data above (Figure 7D), we found that knockdown of muscle MT1-MMP caused a higher stability of aneural AChR clusters against nerve-induced dispersal (arrowheads, lower left panels in Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown in the imaging data presented in Figure 9B.

claim: After photobleaching of aneural AChR clusters in the chimeric co-cultures with MT1-MMP MO muscles cells, the fluorescence intensity of photobleached aneural AChR clusters was partially recovered after 1 day in co-culture.
source: Interestingly, after photobleaching of aneural AChR clusters in the chimeric co-cultures with MT1-MMP MO muscles cells, the fluorescence intensity of photobleached aneural AChR clusters was partially recovered after 1 day in co-culture (arrowheads, lower right panels in Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown in the imaging data presented in Figure 9B.

claim: Diffuse AChRs were constantly recruited to aneural AChR clusters that were stabilized by muscle MT1-MMP knockdown, presumably through the diffusion-trap mechanisms.
source: These results suggested that diffuse AChRs were constantly recruited to aneural AChR clusters that were stabilized by muscle MT1-MMP knockdown, presumably through the diffusion-trap mechanisms in which diffuse AChRs can be immobilized by molecular scaffolds associated with the stable aneural AChR clusters (Geng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation of fluorescence recovery in photobleached aneural clusters, supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2008.

claim: Muscle MT1-MMP plays a dual-functional role in regulating the formation and dispersal of synaptic and aneural AChR clusters, respectively.
source: Taken together, our data further supported that muscle MT1-MMP plays a dual-functional role in regulating the formation and dispersal of synaptic and aneural AChR clusters, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on MT1-MMP effects on both synaptic and aneural AChR clusters.

claim: MT1-MMP was found to be highly enriched at the NMJs in rat soleus muscles.
source: To further investigate if MT1-MMP is required for NMJ development in vivo, we first performed immunostaining experiments to examine the localization of endogenous MT1-MMP at mature NMJs in rat soleus muscles. MT1-MMP was found to be highly enriched at the NMJs (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data from rat soleus muscles presented in Figure 10A.

claim: Some immunostaining signals of MT1-MMP were observed outside of the AChR cluster regions, partly contributed by intracellular MT1-MMP proteins.
source: On the other hand, some immunostaining signals, which were partly contributed by intracellular MT1-MMP proteins, were also observed outside of the AChR cluster regions
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining experiments.

claim: The precise control of MT1-MMP trafficking and surface insertion is required for mediating local ECM degradation at NMJs.
source: further indicating that the precise control of MT1-MMP trafficking and surface insertion is required for mediating local ECM degradation at NMJs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of MT1-MMP signals both at and outside AChR cluster regions.

claim: Pre-incubating the MT1-MMP antibody with recombinant MT1-MMP proteins caused a large reduction of immunostaining signals at the NMJs.
source: The specificity of MT1-MMP antibody was validated by pre-incubating the antibody with recombinant MT1-MMP proteins, which caused a large reduction of immunostaining signals at the NMJs.
evidence: This is shown in the antibody validation experiment.

claim: In 4 days after sciatic nerve cut, there was only a slight reduction in MT1-MMP signals at the NMJs of denervated muscles.
source: In 4 days after sciatic nerve cut, we observed only a slight reduction in MT1-MMP signals at the NMJs of denervated muscles, suggesting that MT1-MMP is expressed primarily in postsynaptic muscles.
evidence: This is shown in the denervation experiment data.

claim: MT1-MMP is expressed primarily in postsynaptic muscles.
source: suggesting that MT1-MMP is expressed primarily in postsynaptic muscles.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the denervation experiment showing persistent MT1-MMP signals after nerve cut.

claim: At E13.5, MT1-MMP-/- mice showed a significantly higher density of aneural AChR clusters than the age-matched WT mice.
source: At E13.5, MT1-MMP-/- mice showed a significantly higher density of aneural AChR clusters than the age-matched WT mice, but the density of synaptic AChR clusters was largely unchanged at this stage (Figure 10C-E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data from MT1-MMP knockout mice presented in Figure 10C-E.

claim: The density of synaptic AChR clusters was largely unchanged at E13.5 in MT1-MMP-/- mice.
source: but the density of synaptic AChR clusters was largely unchanged at this stage (Figure 10C-E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data from MT1-MMP knockout mice presented in Figure 10C-E.

claim: At E18.5, there was a significant reduction in the density of synaptic AChR clusters and endplate band width in MT1-MMP-/- mice compared to those in the WT mice.
source: At E18.5, we observed a significant reduction in the density of synaptic AChR clusters and endplate band width in MT1-MMP-/- mice compared to those in the WT mice (Figure 10E-F)
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data from MT1-MMP knockout mice presented in Figure 10E-F.

claim: Synaptic AChR clusters formed in the MT1-MMP-/- mice were immature with the altered number and density.
source: indicating that synaptic AChR clusters formed in the knockout mice were immature with the altered number and density.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reduced synaptic AChR cluster density and endplate band width in knockout mice.

claim: The phrenic nerve in MT1-MMP-/- mice exhibited abnormal phenotype with less axonal defasciculation and arborization in the diaphragm muscles.
source: Interestingly, the phrenic nerve in MT1-MMP-/- mice also exhibited abnormal phenotype with less axonal defasciculation and arborization in the diaphragm muscles (Figure 10C and G)
evidence: This is shown in the imaging and quantitative data from MT1-MMP knockout mice presented in Figure 10C and G.

claim: The abnormal axonal phenotype in MT1-MMP-/- mice suggests either the retrograde signaling of postsynaptic MT1-MMP or a possible role of neuronal MT1-MMP in regulating axonal growth and differentiation.
source: suggesting either the retrograde signaling of postsynaptic MT1-MMP or a possible role of neuronal MT1-MMP in regulating axonal growth and differentiation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms underlying the axonal phenotype in knockout mice.

claim: The in vivo findings validated the in vitro data showing an important function of MT1-MMP in regulating the recruitment of aneural AChR clusters for the assembly of postsynaptic specializations at developing NMJs.
source: Together, these findings further validated our in vitro data showing an important function of MT1-MMP in regulating the recruitment of aneural AChR clusters for the assembly of postsynaptic specializations at developing NMJs in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: The formation of topologically complex aneural AChR clusters in Xenopus muscle cells requires several key ECM proteins.
source: At developing NMJs, AChR pre-patterns can be formed in muscle fibers without motor innervation in vivo (Lin et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001), suggesting that muscle-intrinsic mechanisms are sufficient to regulate the initial formation of aneural AChR clusters. In this study, we showed that the formation of topologically complex aneural AChR clusters in Xenopus muscle cells requires several key ECM proteins (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1.

claim: The initial formation of AChR clusters may not be solely mediated by muscle-intrinsic mechanisms.
source: As ECM proteins can be secreted and deposited by skeletal myofibers and other different cell types that constitute the synaptic basal lamina at developing NMJs, the initial formation of AChR clusters may not be solely mediated by muscle-intrinsic mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that ECM proteins are required for complex AChR cluster formation.

claim: The synaptic basal lamina contains factors capable of inducing the assembly of synaptic specializations in both presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes.
source: The synaptic basal lamina is unique in composition, containing factors capable of inducing the assembly of synaptic specializations in both presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes, such as laminin-421, collagen IV/VI/XIII, heparan sulfate proteoglycans (e.g. agrin and perlecan), and other ubiquitously expressed ECM proteins (e.g. laminin-111, fibronectin and entactin/nidogen) (Cescon et al., 2018; Chan et al., 2020; Latvanlehto et al., 2010; Singhal and Martin, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Cescon et al., 2018; Chan et al., 2020; Latvanlehto et al., 2010; Singhal and Martin, 2011).

claim: Agrin plays the central role in the formation of postsynaptic specializations by activating the Lrp4/MuSK complex.
source: Among the different factors in the synaptic basal lamina, agrin plays the central role in the formation of postsynaptic specializations by activating the Lrp4/MuSK complex (Kim et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2008 and Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: Extensive degradation of ubiquitously expressed ECM proteins, including gelatin and laminin-111, was observed at AChR clusters.
source: In this study, we observed extensive degradation of ubiquitously expressed ECM proteins, including gelatin and laminin-111, at AChR clusters (Figure 2A-D).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 2A-D.

claim: MMP-3 is implicated for the removal of agrin from synaptic basal lamina at adult NMJs.
source: A previous study suggested that MMP-3 is implicated for the removal of agrin from synaptic basal lamina at adult NMJs (VanSaun and Werle, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to VanSaun and Werle, 2000.

claim: The pattern and intensity of endogenous agrin tracks were largely unaffected by MMP inhibitors.
source: In this study, however, the pattern and intensity of endogenous agrin tracks were largely unaffected by MMP inhibitors (Figure 7F)
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: PLS-associated MMP activity focally degrades different ubiquitously expressed ECM proteins, which clear the zone at the nascent synaptic basal lamina for the deposition of other secreted synaptogenic factors.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that PLS-associated MMP activity focally degrades different ubiquitously expressed ECM proteins, which clear the zone at the nascent synaptic basal lamina for the deposition of other secreted synaptogenic factors (e.g. agrin or neuregulin) and/or dismantle the extracellular anchorage of AChR molecules on ECM proteins that allow aneural clusters to undergo dispersal and re-distribution upon nerve induction (Figure 11).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 11.

claim: Agrin can serve as a mechanotransduction signal, which may transduce ECM and cellular rigidity signals to the Hippo pathway effector YAP.
source: Interestingly, agrin can serve as a mechanotransduction signal, which may transduce ECM and cellular rigidity signals to the Hippo pathway effector YAP, that requires both the Lrp4-MuSK signaling and integrin-focal adhesion signaling in liver cancer cells (Chakraborty et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chakraborty et al., 2017.

claim: Muscle YAP mutation was found to impair the formation of NMJs and to inhibit NMJ regeneration after nerve injury.
source: Importantly, muscle YAP mutation was found to impair the formation of NMJs and to inhibit NMJ regeneration after nerve injury (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: Several typical core and cortex markers of PLSs were highly concentrated at perforated AChR clusters.
source: We detected several typical core and cortex markers of PLSs that were highly concentrated at perforated AChR clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), further confirming the presence of PLSs in primary myotomal muscle cultures.
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PLS cortex proteins may capture MT1-MMP-containing vesicles and facilitate their surface insertion at the perforation and periphery of AChR clusters.
source: At those sites, some MT1-MMP-mCherry signals were captured (Figure 5D), and some MT1-MMP-pHluorin signals were spatially recovered after photobleaching (Figure 6F). These data suggested that PLS cortex proteins may capture MT1-MMP-containing vesicles and facilitate their surface insertion at the perforation and periphery of AChR clusters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 5D and Figure 6F.

claim: The vesicular trafficking and surface insertion of MT1-MMP is precisely controlled to mediate ECM degradation during NMJ formation.
source: These results suggested that the vesicular trafficking and surface insertion of MT1-MMP is precisely controlled to mediate ECM degradation during NMJ formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of MT1-MMP localization patterns using different visualization methods.

claim: EB1 functions to search-and-capture post-Golgi vesicles and to spatially capture microtubules at the cell cortex.
source: Direct interactions between EB1 and other microtubule plus-end-tracking proteins (CLASPs and CLIP-170) are implicated in the 'recruitment mechanism', by which EB1 functions to search-and-capture post-Golgi vesicles and to spatially capture microtubules at the cell cortex (Vaughan, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vaughan, 2005.

claim: LL5β is localized at the postsynaptic membrane to serve as a corral for AChRs within the clusters.
source: LL5β, one of the PLS cortex proteins, is localized at the postsynaptic membrane to serve as a corral for AChRs within the clusters (Kishi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kishi et al., 2005.

claim: LL5β and CLASP1 interact with microtubules for directing the vesicular trafficking of different proteins to the postsynaptic membrane of NMJs and to the focal adhesions.
source: Interestingly, LL5β and CLASP1 interact with microtubules for directing the vesicular trafficking of different proteins to the postsynaptic membrane of NMJs (Basu et al., 2015) and to the focal adhesions (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basu et al., 2015 and Stehbens et al., 2014.

claim: CLASP is involved in microtubule capturing at aneural AChR clusters.
source: In this study, antisense MO-mediated knockdown of endogenous Xenopus CLASP, the homolog of mammalian CLASP1, in cultured muscle cells significantly reduced the local capture of microtubules at AChR clusters, as reflected by the increased average speed of EB1-GFP comets within AChR regions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data from CLASP knockdown experiments presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Microtubule plus-end-tracking proteins are capable to hop on and off from microtubule ends.
source: It was also noted that microtubule plus-end-tracking proteins are capable to hop on and off from microtubule ends (Dragestein et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dragestein et al., 2008.

claim: EB1-mediated microtubule capturing mechanisms can be regulated by PLSs at both cortex (adhesion molecule-based) and core (actin-based) domains via CLASP-dependent and -independent manner respectively.
source: Given that MT1-MMP surface insertion at aneural AChR clusters was significantly inhibited in CLASP-MO muscle cells (Figure 6H), we therefore hypothesize that EB1-mediated microtubule capturing mechanisms can be regulated by PLSs at both cortex (adhesion molecule-based) and core (actin-based) domains via CLASP-dependent and -independent manner respectively
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental findings, supported by data in Figure 6H.

claim: Microtubule-dependent vesicular transport is involved in AChR clustering.
source: which is in agreement with other previous studies demonstrating the involvement of microtubule-dependent vesicular transport in AChR clustering (Basu et al., 2015; Marchand et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basu et al., 2015; Marchand et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2012.

claim: Most nerve contacts in Xenopus primary cultures are located at either the basal surface or the lateral side of muscle cells.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Anderson and Cohen, 1977a; Cohen et al., 1987), most nerve contacts in Xenopus primary cultures are located at either the basal surface or the lateral side of muscle cells, which are influenced by MMP-mediated proteolytic degradation of ECM proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson and Cohen, 1977a; Cohen et al., 1987.

claim: The recruitment of AChRs from aneural clusters, but not diffuse AChRs, is mediated by MT1-MMP-dependent processes.
source: Importantly, we demonstrated that the recruitment of AChRs from aneural clusters, but not diffuse AChRs, is mediated by MT1-MMP-dependent processes.
evidence: This is a finding from the photobleaching experiments in MT1-MMP knockdown co-cultures.

claim: Diffuse AChRs were constantly recruited to aneural AChR clusters that were stabilized by MT1-MMP knockdown.
source: While MT1-MMP knockdown caused a significant inhibition in synaptic AChR clustering at the nerve-muscle contacts, it is intriguing to note that diffuse AChRs were constantly recruited to aneural AChR clusters that were stabilized by MT1-MMP knockdown (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an observation from the photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The recruitment of diffuse AChRs to stable aneural clusters may be mediated by the diffusion-trap mechanism.
source: This recruitment may be mediated by the diffusion-trap mechanism, in which diffuse AChRs can be tethered to molecular scaffolds associated with the stable aneural AChR clusters (Geng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2008.

claim: MT1-MMP facilitates the disassembly of extracellular and/or intracellular molecular scaffolds that are tightly associated with aneural AChR clusters.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that MT1-MMP facilitates the disassembly of extracellular (e.g. ECM proteins) and/or intracellular (e.g. cytoskeletal proteins) molecular scaffolds that are tightly associated with aneural AChR clusters, such that AChR molecules from dispersing aneural clusters can be recruited to synaptic clusters in response to nerve induction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: MT1-MMP is the best characterized and the most prevalent isoform of the large MMP family.
source: MT1-MMP is the best characterized and the most prevalent isoform of the large MMP family, including membrane-type or soluble MMPs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MT1-MMP.

claim: MT1-MMP deficiency causes myogenic impediments and central nucleation of myofibers, which are typically found in muscular dystrophy.
source: MT1-MMP deficiency causes myogenic impediments and central nucleation of myofibers, which are typically found in muscular dystrophy (Ohtake et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ohtake et al., 2006.

claim: MT1-MMP knockout mice develop multiple abnormalities and die between 50–90 postnatal days.
source: Besides, MT1-MMP knockout mice develop multiple abnormalities and die between 50–90 postnatal days (Holmbeck et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holmbeck et al., 1999.

claim: The possibility of functional redundancy by other MMP isoforms is low in MT1-MMP knockout mice.
source: suggesting that the possibility of functional redundancy by other MMP isoforms is low.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the severe phenotype of MT1-MMP knockout mice.

claim: At E18.5, the density of aneural AChR clusters between MT1-MMP-/- and wild-type mice was comparable.
source: However, at E18.5, the density of aneural AChR clusters between MT1-MMP-/- and wild-type mice was comparable.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of MT1-MMP knockout mice.

claim: Aneural AChR clusters in MT1-MMP-/- mice were subjected to the regular metabolic turnover/degradation, leading to the disappearance of aneural AChR clusters at E18.5.
source: While aneural AChR clusters in MT1-MMP-/- mice were not recruited to synaptic AChR clusters, they were subjected to the regular metabolic turnover/degradation, leading to the disappearance of aneural AChR clusters at E18.5.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that aneural cluster density normalizes by E18.5 in knockout mice.

claim: The half-life of extra-synaptic AChRs is only about 19 hr, compared with 8–14 days for synaptic AChRs at mature NMJs.
source: This is supported by previous studies showing that the half-life of extra-synaptic AChRs is only about 19 hr, compared with 8–14 days for synaptic AChRs at mature NMJs (Chang and Huang, 1975; Steinbach et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang and Huang, 1975; Steinbach et al., 1979.

claim: Reduced synaptic AChR density in MT1-MMP-/- mice is attributed by significantly declined recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural clusters and reduced amount of newly inserted AChRs into the postsynaptic regions.
source: On the other hand, reduced synaptic AChR density in MT1-MMP-/- mice (Figure 10E) is attributed by (1) significantly declined recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural clusters, and (2) reduced amount of newly inserted AChRs into the postsynaptic regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the in vivo findings in MT1-MMP knockout mice, supported by data in Figure 10E.

claim: The defects in axonal growth in MT1-MMP-/- mice could be explained by the retrograde signaling initiated by postsynaptic MT1-MMP, which could mediate the extracellular cleavage of Lrp4 to generate ecto-Lrp4 fragments that activate agrin signaling in trans.
source: This phenotype on defects in axonal growth could be explained by the retrograde signaling initiated by postsynaptic MT1-MMP, which could mediate the extracellular cleavage of Lrp4 to generate ecto-Lrp4 fragments that activate agrin signaling in trans (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2012.

claim: Lrp4 is considered as a retrograde signal to induce presynaptic differentiation in vivo.
source: In fact, Lrp4 is also considered as a retrograde signal to induce presynaptic differentiation in vivo (Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yumoto et al., 2012.

claim: Postsynaptic MT1-MMP could mediate the proteolytic conversion of proBDNF to mature BDNF that promotes neuronal survival and outgrowth in cultured neurons.
source: Alternatively, postsynaptic MT1-MMP could also mediate the proteolytic conversion of proBDNF to mature BDNF (Je et al., 2012) that promotes neuronal survival and outgrowth in cultured neurons (Peng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Je et al., 2012 and Peng et al., 2003.

claim: Increased serum levels of several MMPs have been identified in patients with myasthenia gravis.
source: From a clinical perspective, increased serum levels of several MMPs have been identified in patients with myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune neuromuscular disease (Helgeland et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Helgeland et al., 2011.
